title: Product Name Research
summary: Initial product naming research for the AI agent platform.
content:
Product Name Research: The AI Agent Platform

Steffen | 2026-03-15 For Patrik. This is the name that defines the product.

Part 1: What Makes Great Product Names Work

Before generating a single candidate, I studied how the best names in tech were born. Not just what they are, but WHY they work. The patterns are clear.

The Anatomy of Names That Hit

Slack = "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge" was a backronym. Stewart Butterfield picked it because the WORD felt right first. It implies ease, breathing room, the opposite of stress. One syllable. Punchy. Became a verb ("Slack me").

Notion = Latin root "noscere" (to know). An idea, a thought, a concept. It's abstract enough to grow with the product but specific enough to feel like it means something. Two syllables. Warm. Intellectual without being intimidating.

Figma = From Japanese "figuma" (articulated figures/dolls). The founders wanted something Googleable and unique. No one had heard of it. It SOUNDS like it should mean something even though most people don't know the origin. Two syllables. Sharp consonants. Became a verb in design ("Figma it").

Discord = Latin "discordia" (hearts apart). The irony is deliberate: a platform that brings people together named after disagreement. It sounds edgy. It sounds like gaming. Two syllables. The hard D sounds give it weight.

Spotify = Literally a mishearing. Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon were shouting names across rooms. Someone misheard a suggestion as "Spotify." They retrofitted "spot + identify" as the story. The name worked because it SOUNDED right, not because it meant anything. Three syllables. Musical rhythm to it.

Pinterest = Pin + Interest. The founder's wife suggested it while watching TV. Simple mashup. Describes exactly what you do. Three syllables. The "Pin" gives it a physical, tactile quality.

Linear = Named to signify progress. A real English word repurposed. Clean, minimal, feels like the product itself (fast, no-nonsense). Three syllables. The founders were bold enough to use a common word.

The Rules That Emerge

  1. Under 3 syllables is ideal. Slack (1), Notion (2), Figma (2), Discord (2), Zoom (1), Uber (2). The exceptions (Spotify, Pinterest) earn their length through rhythm.

  2. The name must SOUND right before it MEANS anything. Spotify meant nothing. Figma meant nothing to 99% of users. Google was a misspelling. The phonetics do the work.

  3. Hard consonants create memorability. K, D, G, T, P. Slack. Discord. TikTok. Kodak. These sounds stick in your brain.

  4. The best names become verbs. "Google it." "Slack me." "Uber there." "FaceTime me." "Zoom in." The name needs to work as an action, not just a label.

  5. Avoid describing what you do. None of these names are "ChatApp" or "DesignTool" or "MusicPlayer." The abstract names age better because the product can evolve beyond its original scope.

  6. Domain matters less than it used to. Linear has linear.app. Notion has notion.so. The .com is nice but not make-or-break if the name is strong enough.

Part 2: The Competitive Landscape (What NOT to Sound Like)

Every AI agent platform name in 2025-2026 sounds the same:

  • CrewAI, AutoGen, Langflow, Flowise, Lindy, Relay, Vellum, Dify, Glean, n8n, StackAI, Gumloop

The pattern they all follow: Either "AI" in the name, a technical/engineering word, or a generic productivity word. They sound like TOOLS. They sound like SAAS DASHBOARDS. They sound like something you'd see on Product Hunt and forget.

What AOM's product is NOT:

  • It's not another developer tool
  • It's not another "workflow automation platform"
  • It's not another dashboard with a sidebar

What AOM's product IS:

  • A world you enter
  • A team you watch work
  • A place that feels alive
  • The Sims meets mission control
  • Isometric rooms with personality
  • Fun. Visual. Warm.

The name needs to feel like THAT, not like the list above.

Part 3: App Store Name Analysis

Top downloaded apps 2025: ChatGPT, Threads, Google, TikTok, WhatsApp, YouTube, Instagram, Roblox, Fortnite.

What stands out on the App Store:

  • One-word names dominate
  • Names with personality beat names with descriptions
  • Gaming names (Roblox, Fortnite) prove that invented words work at massive scale
  • The apps that feel like "places" (Roblox, Discord, Reddit) have stickier engagement than apps that feel like "tools"

The insight: This product should feel like a PLACE, not a tool. You don't "use" it. You "go to" it. You "check on" your team. You "visit" your world.

Part 4: The Core Metaphors

The product's DNA pulls from specific metaphors. Each opens different naming territories:

Metaphor Feeling Risk
World Expansive, alive, personal Could sound too gaming/metaverse
Room Intimate, personalized, cozy Could sound too small
Crew / Squad Team energy, loyalty, belonging Could sound too casual/military
Deck / Bridge Command, oversight, control Could sound too corporate/Star Trek
Tower Height, vision, strategy Could sound pretentious
Home / Base Safe, central, always there Could sound too generic
Studio Creative, productive, focused Already overused (GitHub, etc.)
Hive Buzzing activity, collaboration Already used (HiveMQ, etc.)
Nest Warm, protective, organized Already used (Google Nest)
Hub Central, connected Massively overused

The winner metaphor: Something between WORLD and ROOM. The product IS a world made of rooms. Each room has a personality. The whole thing is alive. The name should evoke that feeling without literally saying "world" or "room."

Part 5: Patrik's Creative DNA (Informing the Sound)

From me.md and the brand guidelines, Patrik's influences are:

  • Hip-hop, skate culture, 90s/2000s pop culture
  • GTA, Max Payne, The Sims (gaming)
  • 50 Cent, Eminem, Kanye (music with edge)
  • Nike (bold, confident, graphic)
  • SF/Helvetica aesthetic (clean, premium)
  • "Old people can read em, young people love em"

What the name should FEEL like:

  • The confidence of a Nike campaign name
  • The simplicity of an Apple product name
  • The personality of a game studio name
  • The warmth of a place you want to go back to
  • NOT corporate. NOT cold. NOT forgettable.

Part 6: The 20 Candidates

Category A: Real Words, Repurposed

1. Loft Why: A loft is a space above. Open, airy, creative. "Check my Loft." "Open Loft." Feels premium but relaxed. The Sims energy without saying it. Bright, spacious, heaven-like. Domain potential: loft.app, getloft.com, loftapp.com Risk: Real estate associations. May need to fight for mindshare.

2. Volta Why: From Italian, meaning "turn" or "vault." Also references Alessandro Volta (electricity pioneer). Energy. Transformation. Power. Two syllables, strong V opening, satisfying "ta" ending. "Check Volta." "Ask Volta." Domain potential: volta.app, getvolta.com Risk: Volta Trucks (defunct) used the name. May have residual association.

3. Attic Why: The room at the top of the house. Where you keep everything important. Hidden, personal, full of treasures. "Go to my Attic." Warm, personal, unexpected for a tech product. Domain potential: attic.app, myattic.com Risk: Could sound dusty/old. Needs the visual identity to counteract.

4. Fable Why: A story. Every business has one. Every agent has their own story in their room. "Open Fable." "Check Fable." Storytelling DNA. Premium. Warm. Two syllables. Domain potential: fable.app, getfable.com Risk: Fable (the video game series) by Lionhead/Xbox. Strong gaming association which could actually HELP, but trademark conflict risk.

5. Dwell Why: To inhabit. To live in a space. Your agents DWELL in their rooms. "Check Dwell." "Open Dwell." One syllable. Clean. The word itself implies presence and life. Domain potential: dwell.app, getdwell.com Risk: Dwell Magazine exists. Media brand, different space, but name collision.

6. Realm Why: A kingdom. A domain. YOUR realm. Each client gets their own realm of AI agents. "Open my Realm." "Check Realm." One syllable. Powerful. Gaming DNA without being juvenile. Domain potential: realm.app, getrealm.com Risk: MongoDB Realm exists (developer tool). Different audience, but tech overlap.

7. Perch Why: A vantage point. A place to sit and observe. Command center energy without corporate weight. "Check Perch." Birds perch to survey their domain. Elevated. Watchful. Simple. Domain potential: perch.app, getperch.com Risk: Multiple startups have used this. Could feel too small for the "million worlds" vision.

Category B: Invented Words (Sound-First)

8. Tova Why: Sounds warm, human, approachable. Two syllables. Starts with a hard T (memorable), ends with a soft A (inviting). In Hebrew/Scandinavian, it means "good." "Open Tova." "Ask Tova." Feels like a name. Feels like a place. Feels like a friend. Domain potential: tova.app, gettova.com, tova.io Risk: It's a real name (people named Tova exist). Could feel too personal/small.

9. Kova Why: Hard K opening (one of the most memorable phonetic starts). Two syllables. "-ova" suffix feels premium and slightly exotic. In Finnish, "kova" means "hard/strong/powerful." "Check Kova." "Open Kova." Sharp and clean. Domain potential: kova.app, getkova.com, kova.io Risk: Some small brands use this name. Likely clear for a platform product.

10. Plex Why: From "complex" or "multiplex." A structure of many connected parts. Agents in rooms = a plex of activity. One syllable. Sharp. Tech-adjacent without being jargon. "Check Plex." "Open Plex." Domain potential: plex.app (Plex media server exists at plex.tv, so this is likely blocked) Risk: HIGH. Plex (the media server) is well-known. Name collision would be a real problem.

11. Omni Why: All. Everything. Every agent, every room, every world, one platform. "Open Omni." "Check Omni." Short, bold, expansive. Prefix energy without feeling incomplete. Domain potential: omni.app, getomni.com Risk: OmniGroup (Mac software), OmniChannel (marketing term). Overused as a prefix.

12. Vizor Why: A visor is what you look through. A vizor is the one who looks. You're the vizor of your AI world. Two syllables. The Z adds edge. "Open Vizor." "Check Vizor." Strategic, commanding, visual. Domain potential: vizor.app, getvizor.com Risk: Vizor Games exists. Also, "visor" spelling is more standard, which could cause confusion.

13. Mondo Why: Italian for "world." "A million worlds, one platform" = Mondo. Two syllables. Fun to say. Warm. International. Slightly playful without being silly. "Check Mondo." "Open Mondo." Domain potential: mondo.app, getmondo.com Risk: Mondo (UK fintech, now Monzo) used this briefly. Some associations but different product category entirely.

14. Rova Why: Hard R opening. Sounds like "rover" without the baggage. Exploration. Discovery. Two syllables, open ending. "Open Rova." "Ask Rova." Has the same phonetic satisfaction as "Nova" but unique. Domain potential: rova.app, getrova.com Risk: Rova (smart home camera) exists. Small brand, likely clearable.

Category C: Abstract / Conceptual

15. Canopy Why: A canopy covers and protects. It's the highest layer of the forest. You look DOWN through your canopy at your AI world below. Isometric = looking down. Three syllables but flows beautifully. "Check Canopy." "Open Canopy." Nature meets oversight. Domain potential: canopy.app, getcanopy.com Risk: Canopy (tax software) exists. Name collision in SMB space.

16. Prism Why: Light enters, splits into many colors. One platform, many agents, each with their own spectrum. Visual. Clean. Scientific but beautiful. One syllable. "Open Prism." "Check Prism." Domain potential: prism.app, getprism.com Risk: Prism (finance app) existed. Multiple uses of this name across tech.

17. Floe Why: An ice floe is a platform floating in open water. Your world is a floe: self-contained, clean, floating above the chaos. One syllable. Unexpected. Nobody in tech uses this. "Check Floe." "Open Floe." Ultra-clean. Domain potential: floe.app, getfloe.com Risk: Unknown word to most people. Might need explaining. Cold association vs. the warm product vision.

Category D: Gaming/Cultural Reference Plays

18. Pixel Why: The fundamental unit of every screen. Every isometric room is built from pixels. It's the DNA of the visual style. "Open Pixel." "Check Pixel." Two syllables. Universal. Everyone knows it. Domain potential: pixel.app (Google Pixel owns this space) Risk: VERY HIGH. Google Pixel. Too many associations. Would never own the search.

19. Iso Why: Short for isometric. The literal visual perspective of the product. Also "iso" = equal (Greek). Equal access to AI. Two syllables (eye-so). Short, sharp, modern. "Open Iso." "Check Iso." Domain potential: iso.app, getiso.com Risk: ISO (International Organization for Standardization). Strong existing association. Could feel too niche/technical.

20. Voxel Why: A voxel is a 3D pixel. The building block of volumetric worlds. Minecraft, isometric games, pixel art all connect to this word. Two syllables. Unique in the app space. "Open Voxel." Gaming DNA is explicit. Domain potential: voxel.app, getvoxel.com Risk: Too niche. Non-gamers won't know what a voxel is. Fails the "my mom would understand it" test.

Part 7: Narrowing to the Top 5

After sitting with all 20 candidates, filtering through the requirements (simple, clean, unique, verb-friendly, premium, accessible, NOT corporate, NOT jargon, "why didn't I think of that"), here are my top 5.

#5: Mondo

The pitch: Italian for "world." A million worlds, one platform. Mondo.

Why it works:

  • Directly connects to the "million worlds" vision
  • Fun to say. Has a bounce to it. Almost musical.
  • International flavor without being obscure (most people know "mondo" from pop culture)
  • Works as a destination: "Check my Mondo." "Open Mondo."
  • The gaming/pop culture connection is strong (Mondo posters, Mondo Cane, etc.)
  • Two syllables, hard M opening, round O ending

Why it's #5 and not higher:

  • Mondo was briefly used by a UK fintech (now Monzo)
  • "Mondo" can also mean "extreme" or "huge" in slang, which dilutes the meaning slightly
  • It's charming but doesn't quite have the "premium" weight of the top picks

#4: Dwell

The pitch: Your agents live here. They dwell in their rooms. This is where work happens.

Why it works:

  • One syllable. Incredibly clean.
  • The word itself is about inhabiting a space. Your AI team DWELLS in their rooms. The product metaphor is baked into the name.
  • Premium associations: Dwell evokes architecture, design, intentional living
  • Works perfectly as a verb AND noun: "I'll check Dwell." "Open Dwell." "My agents are dwelling."
  • It's quiet and confident. Not shouting. Not trying too hard.
  • "Landing in heaven" vibe, ultra-clean, spacious, bright

Why it's #4 and not higher:

  • Dwell Magazine is a real, established brand in architecture/design
  • One syllable might feel TOO minimal for an app that wants presence on the App Store
  • Doesn't immediately evoke "team" or "agents" or "activity"

#3: Realm

The pitch: Your kingdom. Your AI domain. Enter your Realm.

Why it works:

  • One syllable. Powerful. Immediate.
  • Gaming DNA is STRONG (every RPG player knows what a realm is)
  • Command center energy: you rule your realm
  • Each client gets their own realm = perfect for multi-tenant
  • Works naturally: "Check my Realm." "Open Realm." "Ask my Realm."
  • It sounds premium and expansive without being pretentious
  • The word carries centuries of weight: kingdoms, worlds, domains of power

Why it's #3 and not higher:

  • MongoDB Realm exists in the developer space
  • "Realm" has been used enough in tech/gaming that it won't feel like a "why didn't I think of that" moment
  • It's strong but expected. A good name, not a surprising one.

#2: Kova

The pitch: An invented word that SOUNDS right. Hard K. Open A. Clean, sharp, premium.

Why it works:

  • K is one of the most memorable starting consonants in branding (Kodak, Kia, Kindle, Kayak)
  • Two syllables. Rhythmic. Satisfying to say.
  • In Finnish, "kova" means strong/powerful/hard. Built-in meaning for those who discover it, invisible to those who don't.
  • Completely ownable. No major brand conflicts. Available territory.
  • Works everywhere: "Open Kova." "Check Kova." "Ask Kova." "I'll Kova that."
  • It has the Figma/Spotify quality: sounds like it should mean something, feels right before you know why
  • App Store ready. Website ready. Word of mouth ready.
  • Could absolutely become a verb: "Just Kova it."

Why it's #2 and not #1:

  • It's invented, which means it starts at zero brand recognition. Everything has to be built.
  • No inherent metaphor. Figma could point to "figures/shaping." Kova would need the visual identity to give it meaning.
  • The Finnish meaning is a bonus but won't carry the name on its own.

#1: Loft

The pitch: Open. Airy. Above it all. A creative space you look down into. Loft.

Why it's the one:

  1. The isometric perspective IS a loft. You look down into rooms from above. That IS the loft view. The name describes the EXPERIENCE of using the product without ever saying "AI" or "dashboard" or "platform."

  2. "Landing in heaven" = a loft. Patrik described the site as feeling like "landing in heaven." Ultra-clean, spacious, bright. A loft is exactly that: open floor plans, high ceilings, light pouring in, creative energy.

  3. It works as a verb AND noun. "Check my Loft." "Open Loft." "I lofted that task to Bobby." "What's happening in my Loft?" It's natural. Effortless.

  4. One syllable. Four letters. L-O-F-T. Clean as a whistle. Easy to spell, easy to say, easy to remember, easy to type. Your grandmother can say it. Your 22-year-old designer thinks it sounds cool.

  5. The cultural associations are all correct. Lofts are creative spaces (artist lofts, studio lofts). Lofts are premium (loft apartments are aspirational). Lofts are open (the opposite of cubicles and corporate). Every association pushes in the right direction.

  6. App Store domination. "Loft" stands out in a sea of "AI this" and "Agent that." It's simple, clean, and unique in the AI space. No one else in the AI/agent/dashboard category sounds like this.

  7. Word of mouth. "What app is that?" "It's called Loft." Done. No spelling out. No explaining. No "it's like Uber but for..." The name is simple enough that it doesn't need a tagline to survive in conversation.

  8. The Sims connection. In The Sims, you look down into rooms from an isometric angle. You're in the loft position. The product's core visual metaphor is built into the name without being a gaming reference that alienates business users.

  9. Domain potential. loft.app, tryloft.com, getloft.com, useloft.com, loftai.com are all reasonable paths. The .app TLD was made for products like this.

  10. It's NOT corporate. Nobody hears "Loft" and thinks "enterprise software." They think creative space. They think premium. They think open and bright. That's the vibe.

  11. It scales. "Loft for Teams." "Loft Business." "Loft Enterprise." The name doesn't box you in. Today it's AI agents in isometric rooms. Tomorrow it could be the entire operating system for SMBs. "Loft" holds all of that.

  12. The "why didn't I think of that" factor. When someone hears that an AI platform where you manage your team through isometric rooms is called "Loft," the connection clicks immediately. Of COURSE it's called Loft. You're looking down into rooms. It's open and airy. It's a creative space. The name feels inevitable in hindsight, which is the mark of a great product name.

The Verdict

Loft.

A million worlds, one Loft.

Your AI team lives here. You look down into their rooms from above. The isometric view IS the loft view. It's open, bright, creative, premium, warm, simple, clean, and unique.

Four letters. One syllable. No jargon. No "AI." No corporate stiffness.

Nike would ship this name. Apple would ship this name.

Ship it.

Appendix: Tagline Directions for Loft

If the name is Loft, here are tagline options that complete the picture:

  • "A million worlds, one Loft."
  • "Your team. Alive."
  • "Look down. Everything's working."
  • "The view from above."
  • "Where your AI team lives."
  • "Open your Loft."
  • "Built different. Runs different."

Appendix: Runner-Up Pairings

If "Loft" hits trademark issues or domain challenges, the backup order is:

  1. Kova (invented, ownable, sharp, premium)
  2. Realm (powerful, gaming DNA, command energy)
  3. Dwell (quiet confidence, architectural, lived-in)
  4. Mondo (fun, international, "million worlds")

Each of these could carry the product. But Loft is the one.

Research sources: Slack origin (TechCrunch), Figma naming (WebsiteBuilderInsider), Discord etymology (Medium/Write A Catalyst), Spotify origin (Soundplate), Pinterest naming (Rewind & Capture), Linear about page (linear.app), App Store 2025 charts (MacRumors, TechCrunch), naming strategies (DesignRush, Frozen Lemons, Crunchbase), phonetic branding (JSTOR Daily), invented names (Zinzin, Novanym), AI agent platforms (Marketer Milk, Kore.ai, DataCamp).
